title: MCP 2026-07-28 Specification & Ecosystem Growth
content:
## Overview

On July 28, 2026, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) steering group shipped the **2026-07-28 specification** — the biggest revision to the protocol since its November 2024 launch. It reworks MCP's transport model around a stateless core and formalizes an extensions framework for optional capabilities. This page covers what changed and how large the MCP ecosystem has grown by August 2026; see the Tool Use & Agents page for the original protocol basics.

---

## Stateless Protocol Core

Prior MCP versions assumed a long-lived, stateful connection between client and server (fitting stdio and persistent SSE transports well, but awkward for serverless and load-balanced HTTP deployments). The 2026-07-28 spec redefines the core protocol as **stateless**, so a server can be scaled behind ordinary HTTP infrastructure (load balancers, autoscaling, edge functions) without sticky sessions.

Key mechanics introduced to support this:

- **Multi Round-Trip Requests** — a single logical operation can span multiple HTTP request/response round trips without requiring the server to hold connection state between them.
- **Header-based routing** — session and routing information moves into HTTP headers rather than relying on an open connection, so any request in a sequence can land on any backend instance.
- **Cacheable list results** — `tools/list`, `resources/list`, and similar list operations can now be marked cacheable, cutting redundant round trips for clients (like Claude Code) that re-list available tools frequently.

---

## Extensions Framework

Rather than growing the core spec indefinitely, the 2026-07-28 release introduces a formal **extensions framework**: optional, independently versioned capabilities that a client and server can negotiate support for. Two notable extensions shipped alongside the core spec:

- **MCP Apps** — lets a server return a server-rendered UI (not just text/JSON) that a compatible client can display inline, useful for tools that benefit from a richer response than plain text (e.g., a form, a chart, a file picker).
- **Tasks extension** — standardizes long-running work: a tool call can return a task handle immediately and the client polls or subscribes for completion, instead of holding a request open for a slow operation.

---

## Authorization Hardening & Enterprise-Managed Authorization

The spec tightens authorization to align more closely with standard OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect deployments, closing gaps that had made some MCP server auth implementations inconsistent.

Built on top of that hardening, the **Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension** reached stable status in this release. It lets an organization centrally manage authorization across every MCP server it uses, so end users authenticate once (single sign-on) and that identity carries across all connected MCP servers rather than requiring a separate auth flow per server. Anthropic, Microsoft, and Okta are early adopters, with a growing list of MCP server vendors implementing it.

---

## SDK and Ecosystem Growth

By August 2026, MCP's Tier 1 SDKs (TypeScript and Python) were both updated for the new spec and are seeing enormous adoption:

- Combined Tier 1 SDK downloads are running at **close to half a billion per month**.
- Both the **TypeScript SDK and the Python SDK have individually crossed 1 billion total downloads**.
- Third-party server registries have grown sharply: **Glama** indexes **71,000+** MCP servers, and the **MCP Toplist** aggregator counts nearly **101,000** across combined registries.

This growth reflects MCP's position as the de facto standard for connecting LLM agents (including Claude, via Claude Code and the Claude API) to external tools and data sources — the same role it played at launch, now at much larger scale.

---

## Why This Matters for Claude Code Users

Claude Code and the Claude API act as MCP clients. The stateless core and cacheable list results mean MCP servers Claude Code connects to (GitHub, Slack, Google Drive, and thousands of others) can be deployed more cheaply and reliably at scale, and session startup that involves listing many servers' tools can be faster thanks to list-result caching. The Tasks extension is particularly relevant for long-running agentic tool calls, letting a server hand back control immediately instead of blocking a request for the duration of a slow job.
